name: YARA-X (Rust rewrite of YARA)
baseline: YARA (VirusTotal/yara, the C implementation; the blog calls it 'YARA (legacy)', version not stated)
workload: Scanning files with YARA rules (multi-pattern Aho-Corasick string search plus regex and hex-pattern evaluation): full YARA Forge rule set over 500 random VirusTotal files (about 24 GB); single-rule docs examples (a Bitcoin-address regex over a ~200 MB file, and a for-loop rule).
claimed_speedup: Blog table (500 files, ~24 GB, YARA Forge rule set): YARA-X with daachorse 26.152 s, YARA (legacy) 48.275 s, which the blog states as 'YARA-X with daachorse is 1.85x faster'; the same table lists YARA-X with the previous aho_corasick crate at 57.584 s, i.e. slower than legacy YARA (about 1.19x slower, derived from page data). Docs page: the bitcoin_address regex rule on a ~200 MB file 'will take more than 20 seconds in YARA, but less than a second in YARA-X'; the 'for any i in (0..filesize-1)' rule 'will be 5-6x faster in YARA-X than in YARA'. Both pages say YARA-X is faster in almost all cases with a few exceptions where YARA is better.
why_faster: Blog (about the 2.2x gain over the previous YARA-X build, not directly versus YARA): swapping the aho_corasick crate for daachorse, a double-array Aho-Corasick with a tighter inner loop and cache-efficient storage; a later change groups many 'matches' regexes on one target into a single RegexSet pass. Docs give no mechanism for the regex and loop-rule gaps versus YARA beyond 'performs better ... with regular expressions and complex hex patterns'.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; VirusTotal states it runs YARA-X in production
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: the C/C++, Python and Go APIs differ from YARA's (docs). No process scanning. A few rule semantics differ (docs 'differences with YARA'). Rust crate with C API in capi/.
caveats: First-party claim from the vendor (VirusTotal, Google) with no hardware, compiler flags, YARA version or build options, and the 500-file corpus is private, so the 1.85x figure is not reproducible by others; tier C. The same blog table shows YARA-X was slower than YARA (57.6 s vs 48.3 s) before the daachorse change, and the docs concede a few rules and files where YARA wins. The single-rule claims (20 s vs under 1 s; 5-6x) have no machine, file or version details and are about pathological rules that YARA itself warns on. The VirusTotal Livehunt figures in the blog (p99 over 6 s to under 3 s) compare YARA-X before and after a change, not YARA. I read the markdown sources of the blog and docs inside the repo (site/content/blog/yara-x-just-got-faster/index.md and site/content/docs/intro/yara_vs_yara-x.md), not the rendered virustotal.github.io pages (blocked here).
found_via: Blogs / talks: own recall of Rust rewrites of C pattern-matching tools after the 'rewrite in Rust faster than original C' WebSearch returned nothing specific; opened the VirusTotal/yara-x README, then its site/content blog and docs sources

name: Miller 6 (mlr, Go rewrite of C Miller 5)
baseline: Miller 5, the earlier C implementation of the same tool (the docs explicitly decline to compare with awk, sort or cut)
workload: mlr verbs (cat, sort, stats1, put then-chains) over a one-million-line CSV expanded from example.csv and its DKVP, JSON and NIDX conversions; Miller 5 versus Miller 6 on Mac and on Linux.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in readable text; the results are PNG charts (perf/2026-02-22-verbs.png, cats.png, chains.png). Text claims: release notes 'Performance is on par with Miller 5 for simple processing, and is far better than Miller 5 for complex processing chains -- the latter due to improved multicore utilization. CSV I/O is notably improved.' Performance page: 'CSV processing was particularly improved in Miller 6', 'Record I/O was improved across the board, except that JSON continues to be a CPU-intensive format ... Miller 5 did better than Miller 6 but only on Linux, not Mac', 'Even single-verb processing with put and stats1 was significantly faster on both platforms.'
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.15.15, 1.16.12, 1.17.5 and 1.18beta1 for the 2021 runs per the page; Miller 5 build flags not stated
hardware: MacBook Air with Apple M1 (early 2026 runs); Linux machine not described
why_faster: docs/src/cpu.md: Miller 6 runs the input reader (two goroutines), each verb in a then-chain and the writer as concurrent goroutines connected by channels, so deep chains use several cores (typically 250-350 percent CPU); the page gives no mechanism for the CSV I/O gain.
tradeoffs: Miller 6 is not fully backward compatible with Miller 5 (a documented list of changes). Parallelism is tied to the number of verbs in the chain, so a single simple verb gains nothing. Peak RSS on the million-line CSV `cat` was 379 MB before and 180 MB after the June 2026 allocation work (Miller 6 versus itself).
caveats: Tier D: the Miller 5 versus Miller 6 numbers are only in chart images I could not read, and the text is mixed (on par for simple processing, faster for chains, JSON slower than Miller 5 on Linux). The 'Before/After' tables in the page are Miller 6 against an earlier Miller 6, not against C. Miller 5 is not the C incumbent most developers use for text processing, so this is a same-tool rewrite comparison, not versus awk, cut or sort. Kept as the single notable no-numbers record for this run; the verifier may open the PNGs or rerun scripts/perf/time-verbs.py.
found_via: Blogs / talks: own recall of a Go rewrite of a C text tool; opened johnkerl/miller docs/src/performance.md, new-in-miller-6.md and cpu.md

name: zrep (grep-zg, Zig grep clone)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C); the same table also lists ripgrep 15.1.0
workload: Recursive search for the pattern 'stdio.h' under /usr/include (409 MB, 41K files), warm cache, 28 cores, output piped through cat to avoid a SEEK_HOLE bug on XFS; other modes (-v, -n and more) are listed in the README.
claimed_speedup: From the search-result snippet of the README, normal recursive search: zrep 32.7 ms, ripgrep 38.4 ms, GNU grep 314 ms, so about 9.6x faster than GNU grep (derived from snippet data); the snippet says zrep leads in most of the other modes too.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2 required to build; optimization mode and GNU grep build not seen
tradeoffs: Hobby project by its own description ('how fast grep could really go if you stripped everything away'), so features and regex coverage are likely far narrower than GNU grep; license, build and portability not checked.
caveats: Snippet only: codeberg.org and zff.dev were unreachable from this container (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so I never opened the README, the license, the code or the benchmark method; every figure and the language come from a WebSearch result summary. One pattern, one machine, warm cache. A multi-threaded tool is compared with single-threaded GNU grep, and the 9.6x ratio is mostly parallelism (28 cores); ripgrep, also parallel, is within 17 percent of zrep in the same table. Verifier should open the Codeberg README first and drop the record if the numbers differ.
found_via: WebSearch 'zrep grep Zig ripgrep GNU grep 3.12 benchmark github' after 'command-line text tool written in D OR Nim OR Crystal OR Zig OR Go faster than GNU awk grep sed cut sort benchmark blog' surfaced the zff.dev/imal/grep-zg page
